questions.question: Two independent compound Poisson portfolios have positive rates lambda 1 and lambda 2. When do their pooled severity weights both equal one half?
options: Exactly when their mean claim amounts are equal.
Exactly when their aggregate mean losses are equal.
Exactly when they contain equal numbers of policy records.
Exactly when their arrival rates are equal.

questions.question: Two compound Poisson losses have known marginal rates and severity laws, but their dependence is unspecified. Does the superposition theorem directly justify its summed-rate representation for their sum?
options: Yes; compound Poisson marginal laws alone are sufficient.
No; independence of the component losses must be established.
Yes; dependence affects severity means but cannot affect the sum law.
No; the two severity distributions must first be identical.

questions.question: All component compound Poisson rates are zero. What is the correct boundary interpretation of the pooled model?
options: Total loss has one claim from each component; all weights are equal.
Total rate becomes one so that the weights can be normalised.
Total loss is zero; the displayed rate-normalised severity weights are undefined.
Total loss is random whenever one severity distribution is random.

questions.question: A pooled compound Poisson model has at least one positive-rate portfolio and one zero-rate portfolio. How does changing only the zero-rate portfolio’s severity law affect the pooled loss distribution?
options: It has no effect, because that component has mixture weight zero.
It changes the pooled severity by an equal-portfolio share.
It changes the total arrival rate by the severity mean.
It changes the pooled variance while leaving the pooled mean fixed.

questions.question: Independent compound Poisson portfolios have non-negative finite claim amounts almost surely, but at least one severity has no finite positive-argument MGF. Does this by itself prevent superposition?
options: Yes; finite positive MGFs are a necessary superposition hypothesis.
No; the arrival-and-source construction still gives the law.
Yes; absence of an MGF prevents defining finite Poisson counts.
No; every non-negative severity automatically has a finite positive MGF.

questions.question: Independent compound Poisson portfolios have Poisson rates 2 and 3 and fixed claim amounts 10 and 20. What pooled rate and severity probabilities follow?
options: Rate 5; probabilities 1/2 at each amount.
Rate 6; probabilities 2/5 at 10 and 3/5 at 20.
Rate 5; probabilities 3/5 at 10 and 2/5 at 20.
Rate 5; probabilities 2/5 at 10 and 3/5 at 20.

questions.question: Two independent compound Poisson portfolios have rates 1 and 3. At a threshold t, their severity CDF values are 0.8 and 0.2. What is the pooled severity CDF at t?
Independent compound Poisson portfolios have rates 2 and 3 and fixed severities 10 and 20. What is the pooled aggregate mean loss?
Independent compound Poisson portfolios have rates 2 and 3 and fixed severities 10 and 20. What is the variance of their total compound Poisson loss?
Independent compound Poisson portfolios have rates 2 and 3 and strictly positive severities. What is the probability that their pooled aggregate loss equals zero?
options: $\mathrm{e}^{-2}+\mathrm{e}^{-3}$.

questions.question: Several independent compound Poisson portfolios with positive rates all have exactly the same severity CDF F. What happens to the pooled severity law as their rates vary?
options: It remains F, since its mixture weights sum to one.
It becomes the sum of the rates times F without normalisation.
It becomes a convolution of F with itself once per portfolio.
It becomes deterministic at the common severity mean.

questions.question: Two independent compound Poisson portfolios have rates 2 and 3 and fixed claim amounts 10 and 20. An analyst uses their pooled single-claim CDF as the aggregate-loss CDF, claiming the total cannot exceed 20. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: The bound is valid; a severity bound also bounds its random sum.
The bound fails; arbitrarily many positive claims can give an unbounded total.
The bound fails; total loss is bounded by total rate times largest severity.
The bound fails; total loss always equals one claim from each source.

questions.question: Independent component aggregate losses have MGFs $M_{S_j}(t)=\exp[\lambda_j(M_{X_j}(t)-1)]$ finite at t. How are the aggregate and severity transforms combined in superposition?
options: Aggregate MGFs take equal averages; severity MGFs multiply.
Both sets of MGFs multiply across portfolios.
Aggregate MGFs multiply; severity MGFs take arrival-weighted averages.
Both sets of MGFs take equal portfolio averages.

questions.question: Independent compound Poisson portfolios have rates 2 and 3. The first pays 10 or 20 equally likely per claim; the second always pays 20. Given a randomly selected pooled claim has amount 20, what is its probability of coming from the second portfolio?
Independent compound Poisson portfolios have rates 1,2 and fixed claim amounts 1,2 respectively. At $t=\log2$, what is the aggregate MGF?
options: $\mathrm{e}^7$.
$\mathrm{e}^9$.
$\mathrm{e}^3$.

questions.question: Every component rate of an independent compound Poisson pool is doubled, while its severity laws stay fixed. What changes in the pooled rate and severity mixture?
options: Rate doubles; the severity weights remain the same.
Rate stays fixed; each severity weight doubles.
Rate doubles; the more expensive source receives a larger weight.
Rate quadruples; the severity weights remain the same.

questions.question: Let N be Poisson with rate 2 and set dependent component losses $S_1=10N$, $S_2=20N$. Each marginal is compound Poisson. Which zero-loss probability disproves the independent-superposition prediction of rate 4 with positive severities?
options: Actual zero probability $\mathrm{e}^{-4}$ agrees with predicted $\mathrm{e}^{-4}$.
Actual zero probability $\mathrm{e}^{-6}$ differs from predicted $\mathrm{e}^{-4}$.
Actual zero probability $\mathrm{e}^{-2}$ differs from predicted $\mathrm{e}^{-4}$.
Actual zero probability $2\mathrm{e}^{-2}$ differs from predicted $\mathrm{e}^{-4}$.

questions.question: Two independent compound Poisson portfolios have unknown non-negative rates. Source 1 always pays 1 and source 2 always pays 2. Their pooled aggregate has mean 14 and variance 26. What are the rates of source 1 and source 2, respectively?
options: 4 and 5.
6 and 2.
2 and 12.
2 and 6.

questions.question: Three independent compound Poisson portfolios have rates 1,2,3 and distinct fixed claim amounts 1,2,3. First pool sources 1 and 2, then double only that group arrival rate while keeping its severity mixture fixed. Add unchanged source 3. What are the final severity probabilities on {1,2,3}?
